sourceNotes: Seeded from PEN roleplay performance indicators and entrepreneurship cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: PEN event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the entrepreneurship cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: The process of collecting, organizing, storing, using, and protecting information so a business can make decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: PEN roleplays ask students to explain what information should be collected and how it should be managed.

terms.definition: An attitude that prioritizes understanding and helping customers before, during, and after a sale.
terms.whyItMatters: This term helps students explain service behavior instead of only listing actions.

terms.definition: The process of recognizing an opportunity, organizing resources, and taking risk to create or grow a business.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the foundation term for the event and helps frame most principles-level scenarios.

terms.definition: The willingness to make decisions when outcomes are uncertain and losses are possible.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurship questions frequently connect risk-taking with work ethic, confidence, and venture creation.

terms.definition: Communication designed to influence someone while using clear reasoning, tone, evidence, and body language.
terms.whyItMatters: Principles roleplays require students to explain and persuade in a short meeting with a judge.

terms.definition: A public or private reply to customer feedback that addresses concerns and protects the business's reputation.
terms.whyItMatters: The 2026 PEN judge questions ask how the business should respond to negative customer feedback.

terms.definition: Paying 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of last year's — 110% when prior-year income was above $150,000 — in four quarterly installments, which switches off the underpayment penalty no matter how large April's balance turns out to be.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks how an owner with no withholding avoids a penalty, the answer is this installment arithmetic, not 'set money aside.'

terms.definition: A first-year write-off capped at $5,000 of pre-opening expenses, cut dollar for dollar once those costs pass $50,000, with everything left over amortized in equal pieces across 180 months.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN case listing $12,000 of spending before opening day tests whether the student knows only part of it lands on year one's return.

terms.definition: A flat $5 per square foot of space used exclusively for business, capped at 300 square feet and therefore $1,500 a year, taken instead of tracking a share of actual rent, utilities and insurance.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay about a venture run out of a spare bedroom turns on the exclusive-use test and on which of the two methods returns more money.

terms.definition: A per-mile IRS figure that covers gas, repairs, insurance and depreciation in one number, and it must be chosen in the vehicle's first business year — electing actual expenses first locks the owner out of switching to it later.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how a delivery microbusiness should deduct the car, the tested point is that first-year election, not the cents-per-mile rate itself.

terms.definition: An annual election letting a business expense any item invoiced at or below $2,500 right away instead of capitalizing and depreciating it, so long as the same treatment is used on its own books.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN scenario buying a $900 grinder and a $4,000 oven tests which purchase can be written off this year and which must be spread out.

terms.definition: An election to deduct the whole cost of qualifying equipment in the year it is placed in service, bounded both by an annual dollar cap and by the business's taxable income, so it can never create or deepen a loss.
terms.whyItMatters: Equipment-purchase roleplays hinge on that income limit: a first-year venture with no profit gets nothing from the election at all.

terms.definition: A write-off worth up to 20% of a pass-through owner's net business income, taken on the personal return without itemizing and phased out for certain service businesses once taxable income clears a stated threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing an LLC against a corporation in a PEN case is wrong until the student applies that 20% reduction to the pass-through side first.

terms.definition: The IRS presumption that an activity is a genuine business, and its losses deductible against other income, when it shows a profit in three of the last five years; fail that and deductions are capped at the activity's own revenue.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay about a side venture that has lost money four years running tests whether the student knows the losses stop sheltering wage income.

terms.definition: A single-owner LLC the IRS ignores for federal income tax, so its profit lands on the owner's personal return exactly as a sole proprietorship would, while state law still keeps the liability shield fully in place.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks whether forming an LLC changes the tax bill, the scored answer separates the tax treatment from the liability protection.

terms.definition: Cash a sole proprietor or LLC member pulls out of the business, which lowers owner's equity but is not payroll, not a deductible expense and not the event that triggers tax — the profit was already taxed when it was earned.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay where the owner says 'I pay myself $2,000 a month' tests whether the student knows that figure never appears on the income statement.

terms.definition: The state's revocation of a company's charter after it misses an annual report or franchise-tax deadline, which ends the liability shield and can leave the owner personally answerable for debts run up while the entity was lapsed.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN case about a two-year-old LLC that 'forgot the paperwork' is scored on that consequence, not on the size of the filing fee.

terms.definition: The processor's total take on a card sale, built as a percentage plus a fixed per-transaction charge, which is why a $4 sale surrenders a far larger share of its margin than a $40 sale at the identical quoted rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing a low-ticket item in a PEN roleplay is not defensible until the student works the fixed cent charge out as a percentage of that specific sale.

terms.definition: The multiplier converting an hourly wage into what the worker actually costs, adding payroll taxes, insurance and paid time off — commonly 1.2 to 1.4 times base pay — and it is that loaded number a service job must be priced against.
terms.whyItMatters: Quoting a job in a PEN roleplay off the bare $18 wage underprices it; the scored move is loading the wage first, then adding margin.

terms.definition: The market-rate salary an S-corporation owner must run through payroll before taking any distribution; pay too little and the IRS recharacterizes those distributions as wages and bills the back payroll tax with penalties.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay where the owner takes $10,000 in salary and $90,000 in distributions is scored on whether the student draws that line rather than praising the tax saving.

terms.definition: The window of two months and fifteen days from the start of a tax year in which a company must elect S-corporation treatment; miss it and the business is taxed under its default classification for that entire year.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN case where an owner decides in August to be taxed as an S corporation turns on which year the election can even reach.

terms.definition: A federal filing naming every individual holding 25% or more of a small company or exercising substantial control over it, refiled within 30 days of any change, with a per-day penalty for letting it go stale.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay where a co-founder's stake shifts tests whether the student knows a 30-day clock starts, not just that paperwork exists somewhere.

terms.definition: A buyer-signed document letting a supplier skip sales tax on goods headed for resale, moving the audit exposure onto the buyer — use it on supplies the business consumes itself and the skipped tax returns as use tax plus penalty.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay about a boutique buying both inventory and its own register tape is scored on which invoice the certificate may cover.

terms.definition: Registering a company chartered in one state to transact business in another; skip it and the company can be barred from suing in that state's courts and billed back franchise taxes for every year it operated there.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN case about a venture that opened a second location across the state line is scored on that court-access consequence, not on the registration fee.

terms.definition: A state exemption letting non-hazardous food produced in a home kitchen be sold direct to consumers without a commercial license, bounded by an annual gross-sales cap — commonly around $50,000 — above which a permitted facility becomes mandatory.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay about a baking venture growing past that cap turns on the revenue figure that forces a move into a rented commercial kitchen.

terms.definition: A 5.4% offset against the 6.0% federal rate charged on the first $7,000 of each worker's wages, cutting the annual bill to about $42 a head — but only for an employer whose state unemployment tax was paid on time.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN payroll-budget roleplay is scored on the $42 figure and on what happens to it when the state deposit slips, not on naming the tax.

terms.definition: A flat 24% a payer must hold out of a contractor's payments when the contractor's taxpayer ID is missing or does not match IRS records, remitted immediately and recoverable by the contractor only on the next year's return.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay where a freelancer refuses to hand over a W-9 tests whether the student knows the business must still pay, minus 24%.

terms.definition: Disputed transactions divided by total transactions in a month; cross roughly 0.9% and the card networks place the merchant in a monitoring program with per-dispute fines, and a sustained 1% can end the account entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay about a store with rising disputes is scored on the percentage that triggers monitoring, not on advising better customer service.

terms.definition: A processing quote stated as the card network's own pass-through cost plus a disclosed fixed markup, which lets an owner divide a month's total fees by total card volume and see the effective rate a flat 2.9%-plus-30-cents plan conceals.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two processors in a PEN roleplay requires computing that effective rate from a real month of sales rather than reading the headline number.

terms.definition: The ceiling on the fee a business may add to a credit sale — currently 3% under network rules and never more than the merchant's own cost of acceptance — with debit excluded entirely, advance notice to the networks required, and several states banning the practice outright.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay proposing to pass processing costs to customers is scored on that ceiling and the debit carve-out, not on whether passing costs along is fair.

terms.definition: Whether taxes withheld from employees are due monthly or twice weekly, decided by the total reported over a four-quarter lookback period — above $50,000 an employer moves to the faster schedule, and $100,000 accumulated in a single day forces a next-day deposit.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay about a venture that just doubled its staff is scored on recognizing the deposit rhythm changes before the next payroll runs.

terms.definition: Total revenue divided by every hour the owner works, unbillable ones included, so a solo operator quoting $80 an hour who spends 40% of the week estimating, invoicing and driving is really earning $48.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a PEN roleplay whether a service price is high enough, the scored answer divides by all the hours worked, not the hours billed.

terms.definition: Charging sales tax at the combined rate in force where the buyer takes delivery rather than where the seller sits, which is why two orders leaving the same stockroom on the same day carry different tax.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay about a shop that started shipping online is scored on which address sets the rate, a detail flat-rate guessing gets wrong.

terms.definition: The county or state filing a business must make before trading under any name other than its owner's legal name or its chartered name; without it a bank may refuse the account and some states bar the company from enforcing contracts signed under the unregistered name until it cures the filing.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN case where a sole proprietor signs a supplier contract as a brand name is scored on that enforceability gap, not on branding advice.

terms.definition: Tax charged at ordinary income rates rather than capital-gain rates on the slice of a sale price that earlier write-offs already deducted — sell a fully expensed $9,000 van for $4,000 and the whole $4,000 is ordinary income.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN case where a venture upgrades its equipment is scored on the tax the trade-in creates, which the student must compute against the deduction taken earlier.

terms.definition: The IRS standard separating an employee from a contractor by who directs the method of the work rather than its result, weighed across behavioral, financial and relationship evidence; classify wrong and the business owes the payroll tax it never withheld, plus penalties.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay about a shop that sets a worker's hours and supplies the tools is scored on that method-versus-result line, whatever the signed agreement calls them.

terms.definition: The maximum number of people a fire code permits in a space, found by dividing usable square footage by a per-person factor set by use — roughly 15 square feet each for seated tables, 7 for standing crowds — and it caps ticket sales before demand ever does.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay pricing a pop-up event has to size the crowd from the room's square footage first, then build the revenue forecast on that ceiling.

terms.definition: A zoning approval to run a business from a residence, typically capping the share of floor area it may use, forbidding exterior signage and customer traffic, and limiting non-resident employees — conditions that can rule out the business model itself, not merely the address.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN roleplay about a home-based venture wanting walk-in customers is scored on the traffic restriction, which forces a real storefront decision.

terms.definition: A 100% personal assessment against any owner or bookkeeper responsible for money withheld from employees' paychecks and never sent to the IRS — the one business liability an LLC or corporation does not shield anyone from.
terms.whyItMatters: A PEN case where the owner covers rent with withheld payroll tax is scored on that piercing of the liability shield, not on the cash-flow shortfall.

terms.definition: Copies everything changed since the last full backup, so Friday's run is far larger than Monday's, but a restore needs exactly two pieces — the full backup plus the newest run — against the incremental approach's full backup plus every intervening night in sequence.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-continuity roleplay trades nightly window against recovery speed, and the graded answer is which of these two schemes buys the shorter restore.

terms.definition: Links internal service quality to employee satisfaction and retention, then to productivity and delivered value, then to customer loyalty and finally revenue growth. The practical claim is that the cheapest lever on the customer end of the chain usually sits at the employee end, so a loyalty problem is often a scheduling or training problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Backs a roleplay recommendation to fix rostering or training when the case presents falling guest satisfaction as the problem.

terms.definition: Funding a venture from personal savings and reinvested revenue, not outside capital.
terms.whyItMatters: Many scenarios require building a business with limited resources.

terms.definition: The theory that exchange rates should adjust until an identical basket of goods costs the same in both countries: if a burger is $5 in the U.S. and £4 in Britain, the implied rate is $1.25 per pound, and a market rate of $1.60 says the pound is overvalued. Trade barriers and non-traded services keep real rates from converging to it.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items give two local prices for one product and ask what the exchange rate implies, or ask why a salary converts to very different living standards in two countries.

terms.definition: Tufte's format for comparison: a grid of miniature charts sharing identical axes, identical scales and identical design, with exactly one variable changing from panel to panel - one region, one month or one product each. Holding the scale constant across every panel is the whole specification, and letting each panel auto-scale to its own data is the most common way the format is faked, because it destroys the comparison it exists to make.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-visualization task that hands you five years of sales across eight stores is scored on choosing this over one line chart with eight tangled series.

terms.definition: A Title VII theory attacking a facially neutral policy — a lifting test, a degree requirement, a credit check — that screens out a protected group at a substantially lower rate, with no proof of intent needed. Federal selection guidelines flag a rate below four-fifths of the highest group's, after which the employer must show the practice is job-related and consistent with business necessity. Its neighbour, disparate treatment, requires showing intentional differential treatment.
terms.whyItMatters: Hiring roleplays about a strength requirement that eliminates most female applicants are argued under this theory, not under intentional discrimination.

terms.definition: The mathematical examination of data to identify patterns, test relationships, and support decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors are tested on interpreting findings and drawing evidence-based conclusions.

terms.term: Fair Credit Billing Act billing-error window
terms.definition: A credit-card holder must dispute a charge in writing within 60 days of the statement date on which it first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge the notice and two complete billing cycles — never more than 90 days — to resolve it, and may not report the disputed amount as delinquent while the claim is open. It reaches open-end credit only, so the same $400 charge disputed on a debit card is handled instead under Regulation E's 10-business-day investigation.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law and finance exam items pair this window against the debit-card rule, and a customer-complaint roleplay about a double-billed credit-card charge expects the competitor to state the 60-day filing deadline before offering any goodwill.

terms.definition: Months of survival remaining at the current spend level, found by dividing cash on hand by net monthly burn — $600,000 against $50,000 of net burn is twelve months. Raising prices or collecting faster extends it, while cutting gross spend alone extends it only to the degree net burn actually falls.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a venture roleplay when you should start fundraising, the defensible answer is a month count computed from this division, since a raise takes about six months and must begin well before the number reaches zero.

terms.definition: The value of mutually beneficial trades destroyed when price is pushed away from the market-clearing level by a tax, a ceiling, a floor or a monopoly. On a supply-and-demand diagram it is the triangle between the two curves over the lost quantity — one-half base times height — and it goes to no one: not the buyer, not the seller, not the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask who bears the cost of a per-unit tax and answer with the split of the burden plus this un-captured loss; naming only the tax revenue is an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: The highest-ranking class of motion in Robert's Rules - adjourn, recess, raise a question of privilege, call for the orders of the day - urgent enough that it may be made while other business is pending and outranks every subsidiary motion. Because it does not relate to the pending question it is undebatable in most forms, and its rank is exactly why a motion to adjourn can be made while an amendment is on the floor but an amendment cannot be made while adjournment is.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that ask which motion may be made while another is still pending are testing the precedence ladder, and this class is its top rung.

terms.definition: A situation where two or more moral principles conflict and demand judgment.
terms.whyItMatters: Recognizing and resolving dilemmas is central to leadership and compliance.

terms.definition: A 99.999% uptime commitment, which permits roughly 5.3 minutes of unplanned downtime across an entire year; each nine dropped multiplies that allowance by ten, so 99.99% permits about 53 minutes, 99.9% about 8.8 hours, and 99% about 3.65 days — which is why a vendor's extra decimal costs so much.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay compares two hosting quotes whose uptime promises differ by one decimal, and converting each into annual minutes is what makes the price gap defensible.

terms.definition: Sessions a virtual agent closes without handing the customer to a live representative, divided by every session that virtual agent opened — a bot that finishes 700 of 1,000 chats and passes 300 along contains 70%. The denominator is bot sessions only, which is what separates it from a self-service deflection rate measured against total support demand, so a bot nobody reaches can post a high containment figure while deflecting almost nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A customer-service management roleplay that asks a competitor to justify a chatbot's return turns on this pair of denominators; quoting containment as though it were deflection overstates the labor saved and a judge listening for cost per contact will catch it.

terms.definition: The agreed worth of a venture before an investor's check is added; post-money equals it plus the investment, and the investor's stake is investment divided by post-money — $2 million into an $8 million pre-money buys 20% of a $10 million company, not the 25% a founder computing off pre-money would concede.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship exam item hands you a raise amount and a valuation and asks what percentage the founders keep; getting the denominator wrong is the single most common way competitors lose that question.

terms.definition: The principle that adding more of one input eventually yields less added output.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why scaling operations becomes less efficient past a point.

terms.definition: A written instruction, issued the moment a company reasonably anticipates a dispute, that suspends every routine deletion schedule and directs named custodians to preserve emails, chat threads, drafts and text messages on the subject. The duty attaches before any complaint is filed, and letting an auto-delete rule keep running past that point is what converts ordinary records management into spoliation, exposing the company to an adverse-inference instruction at trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask what an employee must do with a group chat once a customer threatens to sue are testing this duty and, above all, its trigger point.

terms.definition: Charging interest above the legal ceiling a state sets, which makes the loan itself unlawful rather than merely expensive.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the legal line separating a high-cost lender from an illegal one in consumer-credit scenarios, and the reason rate caps exist at all.

terms.definition: A cloud arrangement where the provider runs the hardware, storage and virtualization while the customer still patches the operating system and everything stacked above it; platform services shift that operating system and runtime to the provider, and software as a service leaves the customer responsible for nothing but their own data and user settings.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks who is at fault when an unpatched server is breached, and the answer depends entirely on which of these three lines the contract drew.

terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.definition: An unincorporated business owned by one person who keeps all profit and liability.
terms.whyItMatters: Business structure shapes taxes, liability, and control for a new venture.

terms.definition: Passes a strict two-part test: non-excludable, meaning a non-payer cannot be kept from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is left for anyone else. National defense and a lighthouse qualify; cable television is excludable and a crowded highway is rival, so neither does — which is why private firms underprovide the real thing and taxes fund it.
terms.whyItMatters: Items list several government-provided services and ask which genuinely meets the economic definition; roads, schools and parks fail one prong each and are the intended distractors.

terms.definition: The measured luminance relationship between text and the background behind it under the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, expressed from 1:1 to 21:1. Level AA requires at least 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text - 18 point, or 14 point bold - plus 3:1 for interface components and meaningful graphics; level AAA raises body text to 7:1. Light grey captions and a pale brand colour on a white slide are the two failures that show up most.
terms.whyItMatters: A written event or presentation judged on accessibility is scored on naming the threshold your deck actually meets, not on asserting that the colours look readable.

terms.definition: The function that handles the individual relationship between a business and its non-union workforce — investigations, conduct issues, policy interpretation and conflict between coworkers. Labor relations, by contrast, deals with the collective relationship governed by a negotiated contract with a certified union, so a non-union employer has the first function and none of the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about building positive employer-employee relationships in a non-union business belong to this function, and misnaming it as labor relations costs the point.

terms.definition: The computational discovery of patterns and correlations hidden in large datasets.
terms.whyItMatters: Mining surfaces competitive insights that simple reports would miss.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%. It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: A running ledger of every share, option and convertible instrument, showing each holder's ownership on a fully diluted basis — reserved but unissued options and unconverted notes included — which always reads lower for the founders than the outstanding-shares basis they tend to quote.
terms.whyItMatters: A judge in an ownership-structure roleplay will ask what the founders own after the round; the answer has to come off the fully diluted column, and a competitor who reads the outstanding column overstates the founders' stake every time.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Giving full attention, checking understanding, and responding thoughtfully to a speaker.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect competitors to handle questions and concerns clearly.

terms.definition: Moore's gap between the 13.5% early-adopter band, which buys on the promise of a breakthrough and tolerates an incomplete product, and the 34% early majority, which buys only on references from people already like themselves; products stall in it because the two groups will not act as references for each other, and the standard bridge is dominating one narrow beachhead segment until its references become credible to the next group.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay shows strong early sales that suddenly flatten, naming this gap and the beachhead fix is the diagnosis a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: The final digit of a code such as a twelve-digit UPC, computed from the digits before it so a scanner can catch its own misread: multiply the digits in odd positions by three, add the digits in even positions, and choose the last digit that lifts the total to the next multiple of ten.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-records questions ask how a scanner knows a keyed-in barcode was mistyped without any lookup, and this arithmetic is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: An arrangement granting the right to operate under an established brand and model.
terms.whyItMatters: Franchising is a lower-risk path competitors may recommend over an original build.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: A readability score that converts a passage into a U.S. school grade: 0.39 x (total words / total sentences) + 11.8 x (total syllables / total words) - 15.59. Because sentence length is multiplied by 0.39 and syllable count by 11.8, swapping 'utilize' for 'use' moves the score less than splitting one 30-word sentence into two 15-word ones; consumer-facing documents are normally targeted at grade 8 or below.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to rewrite a return policy for shoppers is scored on whether you can name a measurable target and the two levers that hit it, instead of promising to 'make it simpler.'

terms.definition: Unloading inbound freight and transferring it directly to outbound trailers within hours, sorting by destination on the dock, so the goods are never put away — the opposite of conventional warehousing, which stores, picks and holds stock and therefore incurs carrying cost that this eliminates.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution roleplays about cutting inventory cost and speeding delivery expect this as the named technique, and the judge wants the requirement that inbound and outbound schedules be tightly synchronized.

terms.definition: Normalization's opening stage: every column holds one indivisible value and no table repeats a group of columns across a single row (no phone1, phone2, phone3). It removes repeating groups and nothing else — a partial dependency on part of a composite key survives it, and a transitive dependency survives both it and the second stage.
terms.whyItMatters: A database item hands the competitor a customer table with three comma-packed phone columns and asks which normal form it breaks; the answer is the first, and answering the third throws the point away.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: Short-term debt that turns into equity at the next priced round rather than being repaid in cash, converting at whichever is better for the holder — a discount off the round price, commonly 20%, or a valuation cap that fixes the highest price at which it may convert. Unlike a SAFE it accrues interest and carries a maturity date that can be called.
terms.whyItMatters: A start-up financing roleplay that asks how to raise money before you can defend a valuation is answered with this instrument; the judge is listening for the discount and the cap, not just the word convertible.

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: A letter layout in which every element - date, inside address, salutation, body, complimentary close and signature block - begins flush at the left margin with no indentation, set on one-inch margins with a blank line between parts and no blank-line indents inside paragraphs. Modified block, its near neighbour, moves the date and the closing to start at the horizontal center of the page; semi-block does that and also indents the first line of each paragraph.
terms.whyItMatters: Formatting items on the exam give you the same letter three ways and ask which is full block, and written-event submissions lose presentation points for mixing two of the three.

terms.definition: Freedom from any relationship that would let a firm review its own work: Sarbanes-Oxley bars nine categories of non-audit service for an audit client, forces the lead partner off the engagement after five years, and imposes a one-year cooling-off period before an auditor may join that client as CFO or controller. Objectivity is a mindset; this is the enforceable rule set.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay in which the audit firm is offered the client's bookkeeping work is decided by these prohibitions, not by whether the team feels unbiased.

terms.definition: A structured request that filters and retrieves specific information from a database.
terms.whyItMatters: Querying lets competitors pull exactly the data they need instead of sifting everything.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: A business's capacity to grow revenue and reach without a matching rise in cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges assess whether a proposed venture can grow efficiently.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: A formal written message with a clear subject, correct grammar, and appropriate tone.
terms.whyItMatters: Written events reward mastery of email conventions.

terms.definition: An industry-attractiveness framework scoring five pressures — rivalry among existing firms, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer bargaining power, and supplier bargaining power — where high scores on several forces predict compressed industry margins; it maps the industry, not the single firm, which is what separates it from a SWOT.
terms.whyItMatters: Management roleplays that ask you to brief an owner on whether to enter a crowded category are scored on naming and applying all five pressures, not on listing generic pros and cons.

terms.definition: The stage requiring every non-key column to depend on the whole composite key rather than on one piece of it — a table keyed on (order_id, product_id) that also stores the customer's name breaks it, because the name follows order_id alone. It does nothing whatever when the key is a single column, since a one-column key has no part to depend on.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a table already in first normal form, an exam item asks what still has to be split out; only the partial-dependency test tells the competitor which columns move to a new table.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: A short instrument granting the right to shares at a future priced round, priced by a valuation cap, a discount, or both — but, unlike a convertible note, carrying no interest rate, no maturity date and no repayment claim, so it can never mature into a default the venture must cure.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a financing roleplay to compare two seed offers, the discriminator you must name is that one can come due and the other cannot; exam items test exactly that difference rather than the paperwork.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: An arrangement that puts the main idea, request or answer in the very first sentence and places explanation after it - correct for routine requests, good news, and most internal messages, and expected by busy or senior readers. The indirect pattern reverses that into four ordered parts: a neutral buffer, the reasons, the bad news itself stated once, and a goodwill close. Choose by predicted reaction, not by topic: a refusal a reader already expects can still be written directly.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common written-event error is burying a recommendation in paragraph three of a message the reader will happily agree with.

terms.definition: Each independent layer that performs negotiation work or takes title on the way from producer to end user. A zero-level channel is producer straight to consumer; a broker or agent counts as a level even though it never owns the goods, while carriers, banks and public warehouses count as none because they never negotiate terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a shipping diagram and ask how many levels it has; the trap is counting the trucking firm, which never negotiates and therefore adds no level.

terms.definition: An arbitrary system-generated identifier — normally an auto-incrementing integer — carrying no business meaning, chosen over a natural identifier such as an email address or a part number precisely because the business can change the natural value. When a supplier renumbers all 4,000 of its parts, rows keyed on the part number break every reference pointing at them; rows keyed on the integer do not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on migrating a supplier catalog asks which column should identify a part; picking the meaningful one is what forces the rework the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: Repricing protection for preferred holders when a later round prices below theirs. A full ratchet resets their conversion price all the way to the new low price no matter how few shares were sold; a broad-based weighted average blends the old and new prices in proportion to shares issued, so it takes far less from the founders.
terms.whyItMatters: In a term-negotiation roleplay the two forms look interchangeable on paper and are not: naming which one you would accept, and why the weighted-average form protects the common stock, is what separates a top score.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: A five-step persuasive outline - attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, action - where the fourth step is the one that distinguishes it: the audience is walked through a vivid picture of life after adopting the proposal (or of life if they refuse) before any request is made. A plain problem-solution outline stops after satisfaction, and a call to action without the visualization step is the most common way competitors flatten it back into three parts.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks you to sell a manager on a new procedure, this sequence gives a scored structure; naming the five steps beats an unstructured pitch every time.

terms.definition: A written document laying out marketing objectives, strategies, and tactics for a period.
terms.whyItMatters: The plan guides all promotional and customer-facing decisions.

terms.definition: The enforced rule that every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value that actually exists in the parent table; with it turned on the engine rejects an orphan child row outright, and a delete of a parent must either cascade to its children or be refused, never silently leave them stranded.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a corrupted customer database usually ends with the judge asking what stops a deleted account from leaving unreachable orders behind, and this constraint is the answer.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: A basic first version of a product used to test demand and gather feedback.
terms.whyItMatters: An MVP validates an idea cheaply before heavy development.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: A formal document in standard format used for official outside communication.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect correct formatting, tone, and structure.

terms.definition: Adds items between price or feature points a line already covers, usually to close a gap a rival occupies -- dropping a $600 model between the existing $450 and $850 units; line stretching instead pushes the line past the top or bottom of its current range.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandising roleplay that reports a competitor winning a mid-price slot is scored on filling the gap rather than repricing the whole line.

terms.definition: Keeps every row of the first table and fills the second table's columns with NULL wherever no match exists — those same 120 order-less customers come back, so COUNT(*) returns 500 while COUNT(order_id) returns 380, and the 120-row gap between the two counts is precisely the set that had no match.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to list customers who bought nothing this quarter, the competitor has to name this join and then filter on the NULL — the inner join cannot produce that list at all.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: Allows holders of a specified majority — often a majority of the preferred stock — to force minority shareholders to vote for an approved sale and sell on identical terms, preventing a small holder from blocking an exit. Its mirror image, the tag-along right, instead lets a minority holder demand inclusion in someone else's sale.
terms.whyItMatters: An exit-planning roleplay where one early shareholder refuses to sell turns on whether this clause exists; a competitor who confuses it with the tag-along gives the minority holder a veto that the documents never granted.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: An argument broken into six named parts: the claim, the grounds (the data offered), the warrant - the usually unstated assumption that licenses moving from the grounds to the claim - plus backing that supports the warrant, a qualifier that limits how strongly the claim holds, and a rebuttal that names the conditions under which it fails. Arguments collapse at the warrant far more often than at the data, because the missing piece was never said aloud.
terms.whyItMatters: Defending a recommendation to a judge who pushes back means naming the assumption connecting your figures to your conclusion, which is the step competitors skip when they simply repeat the data louder.

terms.definition: A medium's published open prices per unit of time or space, quoted before any negotiation; national buyers routinely settle 30% to 50% under them, so a media plan costed at these published figures overstates what the buy will actually cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a small client is handed a station's published prices tests whether the competitor knows the quoted number is an opening position, and a plan built on it will look unaffordable when it is not.

terms.definition: Filters whole groups after aggregation, where WHERE filters individual rows before it: 'WHERE amount > 100' throws out small orders and then sums what remains, while 'HAVING SUM(amount) > 100' keeps every order and throws out customers whose total falls short. Run on the same table, the two return different customer lists.
terms.whyItMatters: A query item asks for customers whose yearly spend tops a threshold; putting the test in the WHERE clause returns the wrong set even though the query runs without error.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: A major shift in a venture's direction, product, or market based on feedback.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurs must adapt and justify course corrections when assumptions fail.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: Tufte's distortion metric: the size of the effect shown in the graphic divided by the size of the effect in the data, where an honest chart lands between 0.95 and 1.05. A 20 percent rise drawn as a bar twice as tall scores 5; scaling a pictogram by both height and width doubles a doubling into a fourfold area, scoring about 2. A truncated vertical axis inflates it the same way, which is why a bar chart's axis must start at zero even when a line chart's need not.
terms.whyItMatters: Data-visualization items give a chart and ask why it misleads, and the scored answer names the exaggeration, not just 'the graph looks unfair.'

terms.definition: Identifying and qualifying potential customers who may need an offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective prospecting builds the foundation for successful sales.

terms.definition: A table containing little more than two foreign keys, plus any attribute that belongs to the pairing itself, which converts a single many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships; without it a students-and-courses design has nowhere legal to record that one pair, since neither side's table has room for many values.
terms.whyItMatters: Database-design questions that describe products appearing in many orders and orders holding many products are testing whether you add this third table rather than repeating columns.

terms.definition: Contacts that disconnect while waiting divided by contacts offered — 90 hang-ups out of 3,000 offered is 3%, and most centers exclude calls dropped inside the first 5 seconds as misdials before reporting it. Under 5% is the common acceptance band, and the number rises non-linearly once average wait passes the caller's patience threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand over the offered and abandoned counts and expect both the percentage and the staffing conclusion drawn from it.

terms.definition: Total sales and marketing spend over a period divided by the number of new customers it produced, with salaries, agency fees and tools counted in — not ad spend alone. Blended figures divide by every new customer including organic ones; paid figures count only customers from paid channels and always read higher.
terms.whyItMatters: A marketing-spend roleplay gives you a monthly budget and a customer count and asks whether the channel is working; the judge expects the division shown and the blended-versus-paid distinction stated out loud.

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: Interference produced by the message's own words - unfamiliar jargon, an ambiguous pronoun, a term whose connotation differs for sender and receiver - as opposed to physical noise, which is external to the message (a loud room, a dropped call, small type), and psychological noise, which is inside the receiver (anxiety, distraction, a prior grudge). The distinction decides the fix: repeating the sentence louder cures only the physical kind.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam scenario where a customer misreads a policy term is a semantic-noise item, and the scored remedy is rewording, not resending.

terms.definition: Setting prices based on what competitors charge for similar products.
terms.whyItMatters: It is essential for positioning and staying competitive.

terms.definition: The balanced tree structure behind most database indexes: a lookup descends a few levels instead of reading every row, costing about log2(n) page reads — roughly 20 steps in a 1,000,000-row table where a full scan touches all 1,000,000. Doubling the table adds a single step, so an index worth little at 10,000 rows is worth enormously more at 10,000,000.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a customer lookup that was instant last year now takes 30 seconds, the competitor has to contrast logarithmic index cost with linear scan cost rather than blame the server.

terms.definition: The commitment a company makes about the value and experience it will deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the promise helps employees deliver a consistent experience.

terms.definition: Months needed to earn back what one customer cost to win: acquisition cost divided by that customer's monthly revenue times gross margin, so a $900 cost against $100 a month at 75% margin repays in twelve months. Unlike the payback period on a capital project, this one recurs with every customer the venture acquires.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a financing roleplay why the venture needs working capital even while growing, the answer is that cash goes out to win a customer months before it comes back — this figure is the size of that gap.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: Visual tools such as charts and diagrams that reinforce a message.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must select and justify aids that support their analysis.

terms.definition: The card brands' twelve-requirement security standard, enforced through contract rather than statute, applying to every system that stores, processes or transmits a card account number. Keeping that number out of a system removes it from scope entirely, which is why tokenization shrinks an audit rather than passing one.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail and hospitality roleplays about card acceptance test whether you know non-compliance costs a merchant its ability to take cards, plus fines the brands assess directly.

terms.definition: The share of a table's rows a filter matches, taken as matching rows over total rows: 200 hits in 100,000 rows is 0.2% and the optimizer uses the index, while a filter matching 40,000 of those rows is unselective and a full scan wins, because chasing 40,000 index pointers back into the table costs more than reading the table once.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asks why adding an index on a two-value status column changed nothing; the fraction of rows matched, not the presence of the index, decides it.

terms.definition: Total queue wait across all answered contacts divided by the number answered — an arithmetic mean, so it hides the tail. Nine callers waiting 5 seconds and one waiting 300 still reports 34.5 seconds, while the 80/20 service level exposes the outlier because it counts callers rather than averaging them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-improvement roleplay, the competitor who explains why the average looks healthy while customers complain is using this against service level.

terms.definition: The exchange of goods, services, and capital across national borders.
terms.whyItMatters: A PI targets small-business opportunity in tariffs, logistics, and culture abroad.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: Edward Hall's study of how people use physical distance, mapped to four zones: intimate from contact to about 18 inches, personal from 18 inches to 4 feet, social from 4 to 12 feet, and public beyond 12 feet. Normal business is transacted in the social zone, so a salesperson who closes to 3 feet has entered personal space and is read as pressure rather than warmth. The distances themselves are cultural, and the same 3 feet reads as ordinary in much of Latin America and as intrusive in northern Europe.
terms.whyItMatters: Nonverbal-cue items describe a customer stepping back during a demonstration, and the scored answer names the zone violation instead of calling it 'being uncomfortable.'

terms.definition: The deadline for filing a claim, running from when the cause of action accrued and varying by claim type — commonly two to three years for personal injury, four years for a sale of goods under the UCC, and longer for written contracts. A discovery rule can delay the start until the harm was or should have been found, and tolling pauses the clock during a plaintiff's minority or a defendant's absence from the state.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-procedure questions ask whether a customer injured three years ago can still bring suit against the business.

terms.definition: Deliberately putting back the duplicated columns that normalization removed, trading write cost and update anomalies for read speed: one wide table answers a report with zero joins, but a customer who changes her surname must now be rewritten in every row that copied it, and any row missed is a silent contradiction.
terms.whyItMatters: A reporting-performance roleplay asks why the analytics table repeats the region name in a million rows; the defensible answer is the read-versus-write trade-off, not sloppy design.

terms.definition: The actions a business takes to fix a poor experience and restore trust.
terms.whyItMatters: Recovery answers the complaint and negative-feedback scenarios competitors face.

terms.definition: Lifetime gross profit expected from a customer divided by the cost of winning that customer. Investors treat 3:1 as the working floor for a fundable venture; below 1:1 the business is buying revenue at a loss, and above roughly 5:1 the usual reading is underinvestment in growth rather than excellence.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship exam question hands you a lifetime value and an acquisition cost and asks whether to scale spending; the benchmark number is the tested content, and the ratio must use gross profit, not revenue.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: Albert Mehrabian's finding that when a speaker's words, tone and facial expression contradict each other about how they feel, listeners resolve the conflict by weighting words 7 percent, tone of voice 38 percent, and facial expression 55 percent. The routine misuse is the claim that 93 percent of all communication is nonverbal: the studies tested single words about liking, said by women, in a laboratory, and say nothing about the content of an informational message. Cited correctly, it covers incongruence only.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the standard trap answer on nonverbal-communication items, and a judge who has heard the '93 percent' line all day notices the competitor who states its actual scope.

terms.definition: Treats emotional intelligence as a genuine intelligence with four ranked branches — perceiving emotion, using emotion to facilitate thinking, understanding how emotions combine and change, and managing emotion — and measures it with the MSCEIT, a maximum-performance test whose items are scored against consensus or expert norms instead of asking a person to rate themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that contrast the two dominant EI frameworks turn on this: this one is an ability test with scoreable answers, while the competency model is a rated inventory of habits, and picking the wrong one loses the item.

terms.definition: Splitting one table's rows horizontally across several servers by a key, so four servers each carry about 25% of the rows and the system gains write capacity and room. Replication does the opposite — it copies 100% of the rows onto every server, buying read capacity and failover but not one byte of extra space.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on a database that has outgrown its server asks which approach fixes it; recommending more copies of a table that no longer fits is the trap the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: Time spent handling contacts and wrap-up divided by time logged in and available — 45 minutes of work inside a 50-minute available hour is 90%. Utilization puts total paid hours in the denominator instead, so it absorbs breaks, training and meetings and always reads lower; sustained occupancy above roughly 85% is the figure that predicts agent burnout.
terms.whyItMatters: A staffing roleplay judged on turnover risk needs the two denominators kept apart, or the schedule looks comfortable on paper and burns the team out.

terms.definition: An individual who funds an early-stage startup in exchange for equity.
terms.whyItMatters: Angels are a realistic funding source competitors weigh against loans or savings.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: Presenting numbers and trends visually so patterns are clear.
terms.whyItMatters: Visuals make recommendations look credible and actionable.

terms.definition: Money held by a neutral third party until an obligation is met — in a mortgage, the monthly share of property taxes and insurance the lender collects and pays out.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why a mortgage payment exceeds principal and interest in a home-buying scenario, and why it changes when taxes are reassessed.

terms.definition: The result that a distributed data store can hold at most two of three guarantees — consistency, availability, and tolerance of a network partition. Because a partition is a fact of networks rather than a design option, the live choice is only between the other two: refuse the read and stay correct, or answer it and risk handing back stale data.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a cloud inventory system showed two stores different stock counts during an outage, the competitor has to name the trade-off the vendor chose instead of calling it a bug.

terms.definition: The share of paid staff time not available to take contacts — breaks, training, meetings, absence and paid leave. A center budgeting 30% shrinkage must schedule about 1.43 bodies for every agent it needs live on the phones, because 1 divided by 0.70 is 1.43; ignoring it understaffs a peak by roughly a third.
terms.whyItMatters: Peaks-in-demand roleplays ask how many people to put on the schedule, and the gross-up is where the answer is won or lost.

terms.definition: Revenue from one starting cohort measured a year later — upgrades and expansion added, downgrades and cancellations subtracted — divided by what that cohort paid at the start. It can exceed 100% when existing customers grow, whereas gross revenue retention counts only losses and can therefore never pass 100%.
terms.whyItMatters: In a roleplay defending a growth forecast, this figure is the evidence that revenue compounds without new customers; quoting the gross figure instead understates the venture and the judge will catch the cap at 100%.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: The nonverbal channel of body motion - posture, gesture, facial expression and eye behavior - which is distinct from paralanguage, the vocal qualities wrapped around the words (pitch, rate, volume, pauses, filled hesitations like 'um'), and from chronemics, the messages carried by the use of time such as arriving late, answering after three days, or scheduling only 10 minutes. Naming the right channel matters because each has a different repair.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that ask you to read a supervisor's crossed arms, clipped tone and delayed reply are testing three separate channels in one scenario.

terms.definition: Redesigning a job by loading it vertically — handing the employee planning, decision-making and quality-checking authority previously held by a supervisor, which deepens responsibility. Job enlargement instead loads horizontally, adding more tasks at the same level of authority, and job rotation moves the person between existing jobs without changing any of them; only enrichment changes the amount of control the worker holds.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to motivate a bored experienced employee in a roleplay, adding more of the same tasks is the trap answer; the tested one is giving away supervisory decisions.

terms.definition: Keep three copies of the data on two different media types with one copy held off-site; the arithmetic is the whole point, because a single fire cannot reach the off-site copy, a single failing drive model cannot corrupt the second medium, and one ransomware blast radius cannot encrypt all three at once.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage roleplay about a flooded back office is graded on stating the counts, since answering 'we back up nightly' does not survive the follow-up about where the backup was sitting.

terms.definition: Adjusting communication and approach to cultural and social differences.
terms.whyItMatters: Culturally aware service builds stronger, more diverse relationships.

terms.definition: Profit or loss on one customer or one order taken alone — price minus the variable cost of delivering it, measured before any fixed overhead is spread. A venture can report a healthy blended gross margin and still lose money on every additional unit once shipping, payment fees and support are charged against that unit.
terms.whyItMatters: In a growth roleplay the judge asks whether to spend more on customer acquisition; the correct answer is conditional on this figure being positive, because scaling a negative one accelerates the losses.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: The parliamentary manual whose thresholds get tested: a main motion needs a second and passes on a simple majority of votes cast, an amendment needs a majority, closing debate by moving the previous question needs two-thirds because it takes away a member's right to speak, and a tie fails. Precedence governs order - while an amendment is pending, no new main motion is in order - and a point of order can interrupt because it concerns the rules rather than the question.
terms.whyItMatters: Officer and staff-meeting scenarios ask what vote a motion requires, and the two-thirds threshold for cutting off debate is the one competitors miss.

terms.definition: The number-two or number-three firm by share — roughly 30% against a leader's 40% in Kotler's benchmark structure, above a follower's 20% and a nicher's 10% — which attacks the leader or smaller rivals head-on rather than imitating; a firm with the same share that deliberately copies the leader and avoids provoking retaliation is a follower, so the label is set by chosen posture, not by size alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Strategy roleplays that hand you a share table expect the four positions named and the posture defended; calling every non-leader a competitor loses the distinction.

terms.definition: Striping with parity distributed across at least 3 disks: usable capacity is (n−1)/n of the raw total, so four 2 TB disks give 6 TB rather than 8, and exactly one disk may fail with no data lost. The exposure is the rebuild — a second failure while the array reconstructs the first destroys everything on it.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage-purchase roleplay asks how much of a quoted 8 TB array the business actually gets and how many drive failures it survives; both numbers come straight from the level.

terms.definition: A queuing formula that converts contact volume, average handle time and a target answer speed into required agents, and its output is non-linear: doubling volume needs well under double the staff, while removing the last agent from a tight schedule can multiply wait time. Averages alone cannot produce the answer because arrivals are random, not evenly spaced.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains the counter-intuitive result in a staffing case — cutting one agent from a 20-agent schedule can break an 80/20 target outright.

terms.definition: Share of customer accounts lost during a period, counted one per account no matter how large. Revenue churn instead weights every loss by the dollars it carried, so a venture that loses ten tiny accounts while keeping one enormous one shows alarming account churn alongside near-zero revenue churn.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay presents both numbers and asks which crisis to work on; the judge is testing whether you can say which measure the customer-concentration risk actually shows up in.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: A structured idea session run in four fixed stages: members write ideas silently and independently, then a round-robin in which each person contributes one idea per turn with no discussion allowed, then clarification of each posted item, then private ranking whose tally decides the outcome. Silent generation and one-at-a-time posting are what separate it from open brainstorming, where the loudest member anchors the room; the Delphi technique goes further by keeping experts anonymous across written rounds so they never meet at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Problem-solving group items ask which method protects the quiet member's idea, and this is the process that names how.

terms.definition: Boundaries drawn three standard deviations above and below the process mean and calculated FROM the process's own output, which makes them a statement of what the process does — specification limits are set by the customer or engineer and state what the product must be, so a process can sit inside one pair and outside the other.
terms.whyItMatters: The classic exam trap shows points inside the charted band but outside customer tolerance; recognizing that a stable process can still be producing unacceptable parts is the tested discrimination.

terms.definition: Mirrored pairs that are then striped: usable capacity is exactly half the raw total, so the same four 2 TB disks give 4 TB instead of 6, but the array survives one failure in every pair and rebuilds by copying a single disk rather than recomputing parity from all the rest.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two quotes for the same four drives, the competitor has to trade 2 TB of capacity against a faster, safer rebuild — a judge expects the capacity figure said out loud.

terms.definition: Fully loaded center cost — wages, benefits, technology and facilities — divided by contacts handled; $180,000 a month across 30,000 contacts is $6.00 each. A live phone contact typically runs several times the cost of a self-service session, and that spread, not the software licence, is the business case for deflection.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a chatbot or a help center has to set this figure against the deflected channel to justify the spend.

terms.definition: The state in which demand pulls harder than the sales effort pushes, and it is measured rather than felt: the Sean Ellis survey treats it as reached when more than 40% of active users say they would be very disappointed if the product disappeared, alongside flattening retention curves.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a roleplay when the venture should hire salespeople, the graded answer is not yet if the threshold is unmet — hiring ahead of it burns the runway on a product customers do not miss.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: Standard structures for business documents such as memos, reports, and proposals.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect the correct format for each document type.

terms.definition: Member-governed body that publishes a code of ethics, administers credentialing exams and sets practice standards for a field — the AICPA for accountants, SHRM for HR professionals. A labor union may cover overlapping workers but bargains collectively over wages and conditions; an association negotiates nothing and its only sanction is revoking the credential.
terms.whyItMatters: The accounting roleplay that asks what a professional organization does for a member is scored on services and enforcement, and confusing it with a union loses the item.

terms.definition: Written with dollar signs as $A$1, it pins both the column and the row so the address does not shift when the formula is copied down or across; a relative reference such as A1 moves with the copy, and a mixed reference such as $A1 or A$1 freezes only the half carrying the dollar sign.
terms.whyItMatters: Spreadsheet items give a tax rate in one cell and ask why copying the formula produced zeros further down the column; the missing dollar signs are the graded answer.

terms.definition: Systems and strategies for managing customer data, interactions, and relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: CRM tracks preferences and delivers personalized service at scale.

terms.definition: The short summary of an investment's price, preference and control terms that precedes the definitive documents. Almost all of it is expressly non-binding — only the no-shop exclusivity clause and the confidentiality clause bind on signature — which is why a signed one still lets either side walk away over valuation.
terms.whyItMatters: In a financing roleplay a competitor who calls this a signed deal loses the point; the judge wants to hear which two clauses actually bind and that exclusivity stops you shopping the offer elsewhere.
