terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 index of how far a society's less powerful members accept unequal distribution of authority - Malaysia scores near 100, Austria near 11, the United States around 40. It is a separate dimension from individualism: a high-power-distance audience expects the most senior person to speak first, treats public disagreement with a manager as an attack, and takes an invitation to challenge the presenter as a trap, so a presentation that works in a low-index room must be restructured rather than merely translated.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to adapt a pitch for an overseas client, the scored answer changes who presents and how questions are invited, not just the language.

terms.definition: A Kaplan-and-Norton performance system that reports four linked perspectives — financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth — so that lagging money measures are read alongside the leading operational drivers that produce them, unlike a plain profit-and-loss review.
terms.whyItMatters: Management written events ask how a manager tracks strategy beyond revenue; naming all four perspectives and one measure inside each is what earns the points.

terms.definition: The bit count of a cryptographic key, which cannot be compared across algorithm families: a 256-bit symmetric key doubles in strength with each added bit, while a 2048-bit RSA key rests on the difficulty of factoring and rates at only about 112 bits of equivalent strength. The far bigger number is the weaker key.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-security roleplay asks whether a supplier advertising 2048-bit encryption beats one advertising 256-bit; reading the digits alone gives the wrong recommendation.

terms.definition: Closed cases a customer reopens divided by cases closed in the period — 60 of 1,200 is 5%. It is the audit on first contact resolution: an agent can inflate the resolution figure by closing tickets early, and this is the only metric that catches it, which is why the two are always reported as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-quality case, the competitor who pairs a resolution claim with this check shows the judge they know the headline metric can be gamed.

terms.definition: Annual revenue if every possible buyer bought — market units times average selling price, or the bottom-up count of buyers times price per buyer. The serviceable addressable slice is only the portion the venture's model, licensing and geography can reach, and the serviceable obtainable slice is the share it could realistically win within a few years.
terms.whyItMatters: A venture-pitch roleplay is scored partly on whether the market figure was built up from buyers and prices or borrowed from a headline industry number; the three-tier breakdown is what makes it defensible.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: A readability formula that grades a passage as 0.4 x (words per sentence + percentage of words carrying three or more syllables), so it counts only 'hard words' instead of weighting every syllable the way Flesch-Kincaid does. On the same paragraph the two scores diverge whenever long sentences are built from plain words: a 40-word sentence of one-syllable words drives fog up sharply while Flesch-Kincaid barely moves. General business writing is normally targeted at 12 or below and news writing near 11.
terms.whyItMatters: An editing item hands you one paragraph and two readability scores and asks which formula flagged it, and a roleplay defending a rewritten warranty is scored on naming a target number rather than promising the draft now 'reads better.'

terms.definition: A supplier's promise not to appoint another reseller inside a defined area — a radius, a ZIP-code set, or a named account list — in exchange for the dealer's investment in stock, demo space and trained staff. Since Continental T.V. v. GTE Sylvania in 1977, such non-price vertical restraints are judged under the rule of reason rather than being automatically unlawful, so they stand unless they measurably harm competition among brands.
terms.whyItMatters: A distributor-agreement roleplay asks what the dealer gets for a large stocking commitment; naming the restraint and its rule-of-reason treatment is the legal-considerations point judges look for.

terms.definition: Two different inputs producing the same fixed-length digest, which has to be possible because inputs are unlimited and digests are not. A 256-bit digest has 2^256 possible outputs, but the birthday bound puts an attacker's expected work at about 2^128 attempts — the square root, not the full space — which is why a 128-bit digest is retired and a 256-bit one is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An information-ethics item asks why a system that stores digests instead of files can still be attacked; the square-root shortcut, not the digest length on the label, is the reasoning.

terms.definition: The clock from a customer's message to the first substantive human reply, which stops on that reply even though nothing is fixed yet; resolution time runs on until the issue is actually closed. A 1-hour response with a 3-day resolution is a legitimate and common pair, and quoting one figure for both makes a team look twice as fast as it is.
terms.whyItMatters: Email and social-service roleplays set two separate targets, so a competitor who reports a single number has misread the case.

terms.definition: The first priced round of preferred stock — commonly $5 million to $20 million for 15% to 25% of the company — raised on evidence that revenue repeats predictably. A seed round is smaller, frequently sold on a note or SAFE with no set price, and pays for the search for that repeatability rather than for scaling it.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a financing roleplay which round the venture is ready for, the graded answer is a milestone claim, not a dollar amount: repeatable revenue first, then the priced round.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: The medium — email, phone, in person, memo — chosen for a message.
terms.whyItMatters: Justifying channel choice signals professional maturity.

terms.definition: The portion of total addressable demand a firm's product, price point and channels can actually reach — the total narrowed to the segments and geographies it serves. Narrow it once more by the share realistically winnable in the plan period and you have the serviceable obtainable market.
terms.whyItMatters: Written-event plans that state one giant industry figure lose points; judges expect the total narrowed twice, with the reason for each cut named.

terms.definition: A primary key spread across two or more columns, where uniqueness is broken only when every column in the key matches at once — a key on (student_id, course_id) lets the same student appear 6 times and the same course appear 300 times, but the pair exactly once.
terms.whyItMatters: Enrollment and order-line questions ask how many rows one student or one product may hold; the count comes from reading the columns in the key, not from any rule about the table.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: The preferred holder's first claim on exit proceeds, normally 1x the money invested before common stock receives anything. Non-participating means the holder chooses the preference or converts to common, whichever pays more; participating means the holder takes the preference and then shares the remainder alongside common.
terms.whyItMatters: An exit roleplay gives a sale price below the last valuation and asks what the founders receive; the participating-versus-non-participating split changes that answer entirely and is the graded distinction.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: Scores a passage from 0 to 100 where a HIGHER number means easier, running opposite in direction to every grade-level formula: 206.835 - 1.015 x (words per sentence) - 84.6 x (syllables per word). The 60-to-70 band is the plain-English range consumer documents target, 30 and below is college-graduate difficulty, and 90-100 is fifth-grade text. Because the scale runs to 100, a score of 70 is good here while a grade-level score of 70 would be absurd.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items and written-event judges both hand you a score and ask whether the document suits its audience; reading this 0-to-100 scale as though it were a grade level reverses your answer.

terms.definition: How a product is differentiated in the market and in customers' minds.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear positioning conveys unique value and targets the right segments.

terms.definition: A precomputed lookup of billions of password-to-digest pairs that reverses an unprotected stored password in seconds. Adding a distinct random value to each record before hashing defeats it by arithmetic rather than by secrecy: the attacker must now build one table per record, so 1,000,000 stored passwords demand 1,000,000 tables instead of the single shared one.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why one breached company's passwords were readable overnight and another's were not, the competitor has to explain the per-record work multiplier, not just say the second one 'used encryption'.

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: A single-page grid of nine blocks — customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships and cost structure — used in place of a long written plan so that assumptions about how money is made can be swapped and retested quickly.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks you to lay out a venture in ten minutes, working the nine blocks aloud gives the judge a complete answer; the two right-hand-side blocks people forget are key partnerships and cost structure.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: Letter layout that keeps the inside address, salutation, body paragraphs and any lists flush at the left margin but starts the dateline, complimentary close and signature block at the horizontal center of the page - about the 3-inch tab on a page with 1-inch margins. That one shifted column is the only difference from full block; adding a half-inch first-line indent to every paragraph converts it again into semi-block.
terms.whyItMatters: Formatting questions show the same letter three ways and score the competitor who can point to which elements moved, rather than judging the page by how balanced it looks.

terms.definition: The 2003 federal statute governing commercial email: every message needs truthful headers and subject line, a valid physical postal address, and an opt-out mechanism honored within 10 business days, with civil penalties assessed per individual message sent rather than per campaign.
terms.whyItMatters: An email-promotion roleplay where a client wants to keep mailing customers who unsubscribed is a compliance question with a specific deadline attached, and the per-message penalty structure is what makes a single bad send expensive.

terms.definition: An independent report on whether a service provider's controls actually operated across an observation window, normally 3 to 12 months of collected evidence. A Type I examines the same controls on one single date and attests only that they were designed correctly — so a vendor holding only a Type I has never had those controls tested over time.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay puts two cloud providers side by side, one with each report; the observation period is the distinction a judge scores.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.definition: The initial stretch during which founder or employee equity is granted but not yet earned. On the standard four-year schedule nothing at all vests for the first twelve months, then 25% vests at once on the anniversary and the rest accrues monthly — so a cofounder who leaves in month eleven departs with zero shares.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a cofounder walking out early turns on this clause; without it the departing founder keeps a large stake and the venture becomes unfundable, which is the consequence a judge wants named.

terms.definition: Extra output produced by one more worker, computed as the change in quantity divided by the change in workers. Going from 4 to 5 employees and from 40 to 46 units gives 6. It also sets marginal cost: at a $120 daily wage, that worker's units cost 120 ÷ 6 = $20 each, so cost per unit rises the moment the added output starts shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and productivity items ask what one more scheduled worker actually adds and what that output costs, which is where diminishing returns become dollars.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' pole opposite universalism: which rule applies depends on the relationship and the circumstance, so a signed contract is a starting point a long-standing partner may reopen, and an obligation to a friend can outrank written policy. Universalist cultures - the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Germany - hold that one standard binds everyone regardless of who is asking, which is why the identical request reads as reasonable flexibility on one side of the table and as favoritism on the other.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay where a long-time distributor asks for terms no other account receives is scored on naming the cultural logic at work before ruling on the request.

terms.definition: Open opportunity value divided by the quota for the period: $900,000 of open deals against a $300,000 quota is 3x, the usual rule of thumb for a team that wins about one deal in three. Coverage below the reciprocal of the win rate means the quota is arithmetically unreachable no matter how well the rep sells.
terms.whyItMatters: A district-manager roleplay judged on forecasting expects you to test coverage before promising a number, and to prescribe prospecting rather than closing coaching when coverage is thin.

terms.definition: Combines two tables and keeps only the rows matching on the join column, silently discarding unmatched rows from both sides — 500 customers joined to an orders table returns nothing at all for the 120 who have never ordered, so a customer count taken after the join reports 380 rather than 500.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-analysis item asks why a mailing list built from a joined query is short by exactly the number of inactive customers; the join type is the entire answer.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: Shares set aside for future hires, usually 10% to 20% of the company. Investors normally insist the pool be carved out of the pre-money valuation, which means the whole dilution lands on the existing shareholders — a 15% pool inside an $8 million pre-money quietly lowers the price the founders are really being paid.
terms.whyItMatters: In a term-negotiation roleplay this is the term that changes the effective valuation without changing the headline number; a competitor who negotiates only the valuation and ignores where the pool sits has conceded the point.

terms.definition: Keep producing while the revenue the next unit brings in exceeds the cost it adds, and stop at the output where the two are equal. If the next unit adds $12 of revenue and $9 of cost, making it gains $3; past the crossing point each extra unit subtracts from profit even though total revenue is still rising.
terms.whyItMatters: Factors-affecting-profit items ask for the quantity a firm should produce from a marginal cost and marginal revenue schedule, not from total revenue.

terms.definition: The identity and reputation a person projects through their online presence.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal social media brand can boost or damage credibility.

terms.definition: Fixed costs / contribution margin per unit - the volume at which total revenue and total cost meet and profit is exactly zero. Dividing fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio instead answers the same question in sales dollars, which is the form used when a firm sells a mix of products.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship written event has to show the venture's break-even volume before a judge will give credit for the financial section of the plan.

terms.definition: A state privacy law binding a for-profit business only once it crosses one of three thresholds: more than $25 million in annual gross revenue, personal information on 100,000 or more California consumers or households, or at least 50% of revenue earned from selling or sharing that information. A small firm holding California data can sit entirely outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: A legal-issues item asks whether a startup with 4,000 California customers and $2 million in revenue must honor deletion requests; only the thresholds answer it.

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.

terms.definition: Raising capital from a large number of small investors who each receive real shares and an ownership claim, which makes the raise a securities offering subject to filing and reporting. Rewards crowdfunding sells a pre-order or a perk instead, creates no shareholder, and triggers no securities filing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay comparing two online raises is graded on this split: one leaves the founder with hundreds of shareholders on the cap table forever, the other leaves only orders to fulfill.

terms.definition: Keep the doors open in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; at a lower price closing loses less, because fixed costs are owed either way. At $8 price with $7 variable and $4 fixed cost per unit, the firm loses $3 a unit but still operates, since shutting down would lose the full $4.
terms.whyItMatters: Operating-cost roleplays ask whether a location losing money should close now; the test is variable cost coverage, not whether the site is profitable.

terms.definition: A gesture carrying a fixed verbal translation that works with no speech at all - a thumbs-up, a head shake, the finger-and-thumb ring - which is precisely what separates it from an illustrator, a gesture that means nothing apart from the words it accompanies, such as sketching a package's size in the air. Because the translation is assigned by culture rather than by resemblance, this type can invert across a border: the same ring means money in Japan and is obscene in Brazil.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay that has you demonstrate a product to a foreign buyer is scored on choosing gestures whose meaning does not flip, and exam items ask which gesture type still communicates when used silently.

terms.definition: The claim history report an insurer issues listing every claim in a period with its date, amounts paid and any reserve still open. Brokers price renewals from it and use it to prove a firm's record when moving carriers, so reserves left open on settled claims quietly inflate the next quote.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about shopping a client's coverage starts by pulling this report; asking for it shows the judge you know renewals are priced from history, not from a sales pitch.

terms.definition: The legally fixed span between learning of a personal-data breach and having to report it — 72 hours to the supervising authority under EU rules, with U.S. state statutes commonly allowing 30 to 60 days for notice to the individuals affected. The clock starts at awareness, not at the intrusion, so an attack that sat undetected for 8 months still leaves the full window intact once it is found.
terms.whyItMatters: An incident roleplay asks when the company is late; competitors who count from the intrusion date report the firm as months overdue when it is in fact on day one.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: A loan made by an ordinary bank that the Small Business Administration guarantees against default — 85% of the balance on loans up to $150,000 and 75% above that, to a $5 million ceiling. The guarantee is what persuades a lender to accept a borrower whose collateral and operating history would otherwise be too thin.
terms.whyItMatters: In a financing roleplay for a start-up that a bank has already declined, naming this program and the guarantee percentage is the concrete recommendation a judge is waiting for.

terms.definition: Selling price multiplied by the extra output the next worker adds — $15 a unit times 6 units is $90 a day. Hire while that figure is at or above the wage and stop when it drops below: at a $100 wage this worker is not worth adding, even though the worker before, adding 9 units and $135, clearly was.
terms.whyItMatters: Labor and productivity questions ask how many people a firm should employ, and the comparison of this figure to the wage is the tested rule.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of whether people define themselves as 'I' or as part of a permanent in-group: the United States scores about 91, the highest of the fifty-plus countries surveyed, and Guatemala about 6. It answers a different question than power distance, which measures tolerance of unequal authority, and a country can be strongly collectivist while low in power distance. The communication consequence differs accordingly - a high score licenses naming one person's contribution and negotiating one-to-one, a low score requires the group to settle a position before any single voice states it.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking why singling out one employee for praise backfired with an overseas team is scored on this dimension, not on generic 'cultural differences.'

terms.definition: An obligation under the Americans with Disabilities Act, which covers employers with 15 or more employees, to adjust a job or workplace — modified schedule, assistive equipment, reassignment to a vacant role — so a qualified individual can perform the essential functions of the position. It is triggered by a request, worked out through an interactive process, and limited by undue hardship measured against the employer's overall size and resources rather than one department's budget.
terms.whyItMatters: HR roleplays about a schedule change request are scored on the interactive process and the undue-hardship limit, not on sympathy.

terms.definition: Pairs every row of one table with every row of another under no condition at all, so the output is m × n rows — 50 products against 12 months yields 600. A two-table query whose join condition is left off collapses into one, which is how a query over 1,000 and 2,000 rows returns 2,000,000 and freezes the report.
terms.whyItMatters: A troubleshooting item shows a report that suddenly returns millions of rows from two small tables; the multiplication, not the data, explains it.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: The pre-contract document sketching a deal's outline, in which price and structure are expressly non-binding but the exclusivity, confidentiality and expense-allocation clauses bind the moment it is signed — so it is emphatically not the harmless handshake its informal tone suggests.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-sale roleplay where the seller wants to keep talking to another buyer turns on which clauses in this document survive; the judge is testing whether you know price is the part that does not bind.

terms.definition: The smallest output at which long-run average cost stops falling and flattens out. If unit cost drops from $9 to $6 between 10,000 and 50,000 units and then holds at $6, the threshold is 50,000 — a rival producing 20,000 pays $7 or $8 and cannot match a $6.50 price, which is how the number becomes an entry barrier.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition items ask why a small entrant cannot match an incumbent's price, and the expected answer is the output threshold, not brand loyalty.

terms.definition: A short opening section of a report that distills key findings and recommendations.
terms.whyItMatters: Written events reward a crisp, decision-ready summary.

terms.definition: Emotional self-perception measured as a personality disposition: instruments such as the TEIQue ask a person to agree or disagree with statements about themselves across roughly fifteen facets, so the score records self-belief and overlaps heavily with the Big Five. Ability EI, by contrast, is scored on correct answers to emotion problems, which is why the two kinds of measure correlate only weakly with each other.
terms.whyItMatters: A human resources roleplay in which a candidate proposes an EI screen for hiring is judged on knowing that a self-report inventory can be gamed by an applicant while a performance test cannot.

terms.definition: The 128-bit addressing scheme succeeding the 32-bit scheme the internet was built on. Because each added bit doubles the space, 128 bits is not four times larger but 2^96 times larger — the older scheme's roughly 4.3 billion addresses ran out, and the newer one is written as eight hexadecimal groups rather than four decimal ones.
terms.whyItMatters: An item on the scope of the internet asks why address exhaustion forced a change instead of an expansion; the doubling, not the label, is the explanation.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: The 23-item filing a franchisor must place in a prospect's hands at least 14 calendar days before any money changes hands or any agreement is signed. Its items cover fees, litigation and bankruptcy history, territory rights, and the roster of current franchisees plus everyone who left in the past three years.
terms.whyItMatters: A franchise-purchase roleplay is scored on whether you use the waiting period to call former franchisees; a competitor who signs on the spot has skipped the protection the rule exists to give.

terms.definition: Gap between what buyers would have paid and what they did pay, measured as the area under the demand curve and above the market price. With demand starting at $50, a $20 price and 300 units sold, it equals ½ × 300 × ($50 − $20) = $4,500 — and a price rise to $30 cuts it, which is the value a seller captures when it segments buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-function questions ask what buyers lose when a price rises or a shortage appears; the triangle turns that into a dollar figure.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of how threatened a culture feels by ambiguity, which predicts how much written structure a message must carry: high scorers such as Greece near 100 and Japan near 92 expect detailed agendas, explicit rules and signed detail before acting, while low scorers such as Singapore near 8 and Denmark near 23 will work from an open-ended proposal. It is not risk aversion in the financial sense - a high-scoring culture may take a very large risk, provided the procedure for taking it is spelled out.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how to prepare for a first meeting with a Japanese partner is scored on sending the agenda and documentation in advance rather than planning to improvise.

terms.definition: A court-supervised liquidation discharging most unsecured debts by selling non-exempt assets, unlike a Chapter 13 filing, which keeps assets under a multi-year repayment plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Debt-control scenarios test that student loans and most taxes survive discharge, and that the filing sits on a credit report for a decade.

terms.definition: A 32-bit pattern splitting an address into a network part and a host part: a /24 leaves 8 bits for hosts, which is 2^8 = 256 addresses, of which 254 are assignable once the network and broadcast addresses come out. A /25 halves that to 126 usable, so borrowing a single bit costs half the room on the segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how many devices a store's network segment can hold, the competitor must convert the slash number into host bits and then subtract 2 — the raw power of two is the wrong answer.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: The SEC exemption that lets a company raise up to $5 million in any twelve months from the general public through a registered funding portal, capping how much a non-accredited investor may put in based on their income and net worth, and obliging the issuer to file annual reports afterward.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a financing roleplay whether the venture can simply ask the public for money, the answer is yes but only inside this exemption — the ceiling and the ongoing reporting duty are the tested details.

terms.definition: Area between the equal-shares diagonal and the actual income curve, divided by the whole triangle under that diagonal, giving 0 for identical incomes and 1 for one household holding everything. A move from 0.38 to 0.45 means income concentrated, and since it is a ratio it says nothing about whether anyone got richer.
terms.whyItMatters: Economic-development items compare two markets' income spread to pick a target segment, and the score is the measure they hand you.

terms.definition: Sorts national communication styles into three categories rather than scoring dimensions: linear-active cultures (Germany, Switzerland, the U.S.) plan sequentially, do one thing at a time and argue from facts; multi-active cultures (Italy, Brazil, much of Africa) speak over one another, run several tasks at once and put the relationship ahead of the schedule; reactive cultures (Japan, China, Finland) listen first, do not interrupt, and answer only after a silence that outsiders misread as disagreement. Each country lands in one category, which is what makes it usable mid-meeting where a six-dimension score is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay in which the counterpart falls silent after your proposal is scored on reading the pause as a reactive-style norm instead of filling it with an unnecessary concession.

terms.definition: The half of a job-analysis output that describes the person rather than the work — required education, licensure, years of experience, skills and physical requirements. Its companion, the job description, lists the duties, reporting relationship and working conditions of the position itself; a screening decision must be traceable to the specification, because a requirement that appears nowhere in it is very hard to defend as job related.
terms.whyItMatters: Building a posting in a hiring roleplay is scored on separating what the job does from what the person must bring, which is where invented requirements get caught.

terms.definition: Hits divided by total lookups — 900 of 1,000 is 90%. Read as percentage points the figure misleads: moving from 90% to 95% cuts the 100 misses that reach the database down to 50, so a five-point gain halves backend load, and the last few points are worth far more than the first.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks whether a small improvement to a caching layer is worth the spend; the answer runs on misses removed, not on the headline percentage.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Capital repaid as a fixed slice of monthly revenue — commonly 3% to 8% — until a set multiple of the advance, usually 1.3x to 1.5x, has been returned. There is no fixed maturity date the way a term loan has one, and no ownership is given up the way an equity round would require.
terms.whyItMatters: In a financing roleplay for a venture with steady revenue but no collateral, this is the recommendation that avoids both dilution and a fixed payment the slow months cannot cover.

terms.definition: Allocate a budget so the last dollar spent on each good returns the same added satisfaction: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. If one item returns 20 utils per dollar and another 10, shifting spending toward the first raises total satisfaction until the two ratios meet — the rule that produces the downward-sloping demand curve.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior roleplays ask why a shopper walked away from the better product; the per-dollar comparison, not the raw benefit, explains the switch.

terms.definition: The point inside a speaker's turn - a completed clause, a finished idea, a falling intonation - at which someone else may take the floor without it counting as an interruption. Conversation analysis clocks the median gap between turns at about 200 milliseconds across languages, so speech beginning before one of these points is an interruption while speech beginning at one is a harmless overlap, and a silence stretched past roughly 700 milliseconds is itself heard as reluctance or disagreement.
terms.whyItMatters: Group-discussion and team-event judges score whether a competitor gets into the conversation without cutting anyone off, which is a finer rule than 'wait until they stop talking.'

terms.definition: Optimizes the discounted value of a customer's entire future stream of purchases and will accept a thinner margin on any single sale to protect it, whereas transactional marketing maximizes margin on each separate exchange and budgets acquisition and retention as unrelated lines; the two approaches give opposite answers to whether a long-standing customer should be granted a concession on one order.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a loyal customer asks for an exception is decided by which of the two frames you argue from, and judges expect the alternative named.

terms.definition: The 1,024-based unit an operating system counts in, set against the 1,000-based unit a drive is sold in: a '1 TB' disk holds 10^12 bytes, but the OS divides by 1,024 three times and reports 931 GB — a 7% shortfall that widens at every prefix step, so a 4 TB drive shows as 3.64 TB, roughly 9% short.
terms.whyItMatters: A records-storage item asks how many years of files a purchased drive really holds; sizing the archive off the number on the box overstates capacity before the first backup runs.
